claims.text: Chemical short-range order typically suppresses lattice thermal conductivity in concentrated refractory high-entropy alloys relative to a random solid solution.
The conductivity suppression is caused by enhanced phonon scattering at SRO domain boundaries and within SRO regions.
The magnitude of conductivity suppression depends on SRO correlation length and atomic mass variance.
Rapid quenching from high temperature suppresses SRO and produces an RSS reference state.
Intermediate-temperature aging at 0.5–0.7 Tm promotes local SRO without causing phase separation or long-range ordering.
Mo-Nb-Ta-V-W RHEAs exhibit SRO with a correlation length of 1–2 nm.
The relevant SRO volume fraction is 10–30%.
SRO in MoNbTaW can generate diffuse antiphase boundaries.
SRO domains generate local strain fields that disrupt phonon propagation.
Local compositional fluctuations within SRO regions produce additional mass-difference phonon scattering.
Lattice distortions at SRO domain boundaries produce additional strain-field phonon scattering.
Localized vibrational modes in ordered clusters produce resonant phonon scattering.
SRO-related scattering increases with correlation length up to approximately 2 nm, then saturates or decreases as larger domains begin to support coherent phonon transport.
At room temperature, SRO lowers lattice thermal conductivity by 15–40% relative to an RSS of the same composition.
SRO-induced conductivity suppression diminishes above 1000 K because anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering becomes dominant.
SRO has a stronger conductivity-suppressing effect in alloys with larger atomic mass variance, including W-containing alloys.
The proposed effect is strongest when the SRO correlation length is comparable to a phonon mean free path of 1–5 nm.
The hypothesis applies to single-phase BCC or FCC RHEAs without precipitation or long-range ordering and does not apply when SRO triggers secondary phases or long-range order.
